overview.text: The Khmer Rouge was the radical communist movement that ruled Cambodia, then called Democratic Kampuchea, from April 1975 to January 1979. Its leaders, including Pol Pot, tried to remake society through forced agricultural labor and tight political control. After taking Phnom Penh, the movement emptied cities and moved residents into the countryside. Executions, imprisonment, hunger, disease, and harsh work killed an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people; ethnic minorities also faced persecution. Vietnamese forces overthrew the regime in 1979. Decades later, a Cambodian-United Nations tribunal investigated senior leaders and major perpetrators. The term “Khmer Rouge” names the movement and regime, not the Cambodian people as a whole.

overview.text: The Stolen Generations are Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who, as children, were forcibly separated from their families under Australian government removal policies and institutional practices. Many were placed in institutions or non-Indigenous homes, disrupting family ties, language, and culture. Removal occurred across different jurisdictions and periods, so no single date describes every person's experience. Australia's 1997 Bringing Them Home inquiry documented the laws and practices behind these removals, recorded personal testimony, and recommended healing and reconciliation measures. In February 2008, Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologized in Parliament to the Stolen Generations. Survivors and descendants continue to describe lasting effects, including grief and intergenerational trauma.

overview.text: The Assyrian Empire grew from northern Mesopotamia and became one of the dominant powers of the ancient Near East in the first millennium BCE. Its rulers moved their capital several times, from the traditional center of Ashur to cities including Nimrud and, under Sennacherib, Nineveh. Palace reliefs at Nineveh depict royal campaigns and ceremonies, revealing how kings presented their power. Ashurbanipal assembled a major collection of cuneiform texts there. Assyrian control at its height reached as far as Egypt. A Babylonian-Median coalition sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE; a remnant Assyrian state survived briefly afterward. The empire is remembered through both its military expansion and its preserved art and written records.

key_facts.text: Ashur was an early capital; Sennacherib later made Nineveh the imperial capital.
Nineveh lay in northern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq.
Nineveh’s palace reliefs portrayed campaigns, royal ceremonies, and protective figures.
Ashurbanipal gathered a major cuneiform library at Nineveh.
Nineveh fell in 612 BCE, though Assyrian resistance continued until 605 BCE.

overview.text: Maria Theresa ruled the Habsburg hereditary lands from 1740 to 1780 after inheriting them from her father, Emperor Charles VI. Other European powers challenged that succession, starting the War of the Austrian Succession. Frederick II of Prussia seized Silesia, which Maria Theresa ultimately had to cede. The shock of war helped spur reforms in administration and the army. Her reign also saw wider modernization of the Habsburg state, although her attitude toward Enlightenment ideas was cautious and she was intolerant of some religious communities. Her son Joseph II later continued reforms, first as her co-ruler and then on his own. Maria Theresa herself was not Holy Roman emperor.

overview.text: Louis XVI was the Bourbon king of France when the French Revolution began. He inherited the throne in 1774 and faced deep financial problems. In May 1789 he summoned the Estates General to Versailles; disputes over representation and power helped turn that assembly into a revolutionary crisis. Popular pressure forced Louis and his wife, Marie Antoinette, to leave Versailles for Paris later that year. The monarchy was abolished in 1792, and Louis was tried by the National Convention. He was executed by guillotine on January 21, 1793. His fall illustrates how the revolution moved from demands for reform of monarchy to the creation of a republic.

overview.text: The European Union is a political and economic partnership whose modern legal form came from the Maastricht Treaty. Six western European countries began earlier cooperation in coal and steel, then created the European Economic Community through the 1957 Treaties of Rome. Maastricht was signed in 1992 and entered into force on November 1, 1993, formally establishing the EU on the foundations of those communities. It expanded cooperation to foreign policy, justice, and home affairs and introduced EU citizenship. A single market supports movement of goods, services, people, and capital. The euro cash changeover began in 2002 for participating countries; EU membership and use of the euro are not identical.

overview.text: The Congo Free State was a central African territory ruled personally by Belgium's King Leopold II from 1885 until Belgium took it over in 1908. It covered much of today's Democratic Republic of the Congo, but it was not initially a colony of the Belgian state. Leopold's administration claimed uncultivated land and granted concessions to companies that extracted ivory and rubber. Those companies imposed forced labor, often under inhumane conditions, and the regime became notorious for violence and other abuses. Reports of mistreatment drew international outrage. Belgium annexed the territory in November 1908, ending the Free State and beginning a different colonial administration. Its name “Free State” concealed coercive rule.

overview.text: The Zulu are a southern African people whose language, isiZulu, belongs to the Nguni group. Their history includes the rise of a powerful kingdom in the early nineteenth century, when Shaka brought many chiefdoms under centralized rule and reorganized military forces. The kingdom survived his death in 1828. Under King Cetshwayo, it resisted British demands to disarm, and Britain invaded Zululand in 1879. The Anglo-Zulu War included the Battle of Isandlwana, where Zulu forces defeated a British column, before British forces won at Ulundi and subsequently divided the kingdom. Zulu communities and language continue today; the people should not be reduced to the history of one king or one war.

overview.text: Leonidas I was a king of Sparta who commanded a Greek coalition at Thermopylae in 480 BCE during the Persian invasion led by Xerxes I. The narrow coastal pass helped the defenders resist a much larger army for several days. The famous 300 Spartan soldiers were only part of the Greek force, which also included troops from other city-states. After Persian forces found a mountain route around the pass, most Greek troops withdrew while Leonidas and a smaller rearguard remained. Leonidas died in the final fighting. The defeat opened the route southward for the Persians, but Greek resistance continued, including later victories at Salamis and Plataea.

overview.text: Chichén Itzá was a major Maya city on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, built near natural sinkholes called cenotes that supplied access to water. Its surviving monuments combine Maya building traditions with influences from central Mexico. El Castillo, also called the Temple of Kukulcán, rises above the main plaza; the Great Ball Court, Temple of the Warriors, and sacred cenote are other prominent features. The ball court's stone rings and reliefs show that the game had ceremonial as well as athletic meaning. UNESCO recognizes the city as World Heritage for its architecture and regional influence. Its monuments reveal several phases of construction and cultural exchange across the region.
